mn26:1.2: at one time the Fortunate One was dwelling near Sāvatthī at Anāthapiṇḍika’s grounds in Jeta’s Wood.
mn26:2.1: Then the Fortunate One, having dressed in the morning time, after picking up his bowl and robe, was entering Sāvatthī for alms.
mn26:2.2: Then many monks approached venerable Ānanda, and after approaching, they said this to venerable Ānanda:
mn26:2.3: “It has been a long time, friend Ānanda, since we heard talk about the Dhamma face to face with the Fortunate One.
mn26:2.4: It would be good, friend Ānanda, if we were to get to listen to talk about the Dhamma face to face with the Fortunate One.”
mn26:2.5: “Then, venerables, please approach the brāhmaṇa Rammaka’s hermitage,
mn26:2.6: it would be well if you get to listen to talk about the Dhamma face to face with the Fortunate One.”
mn26:2.7: “Yes, venerable,” those monks replied to venerable Ānanda.
mn26:3.1: Then the Fortunate One, after walking for alms in Sāvatthī, and returning from the alms-round after the meal, addressed venerable Ānanda, saying:
mn26:3.2: “Come Ānanda, let us approach the Eastern Monastery and Migāra’s mother’s mansion to spend the day.”
mn26:3.3: “Very well, reverend Sir,” venerable Ānanda replied to the Fortunate One.
mn26:3.4: Then the Fortunate One, together with venerable Ānanda, approached the Eastern Monastery and Migāra’s mother’s mansion to spend the day.
mn26:3.5: Then the Fortunate One, having risen from seclusion in the evening time, addressed venerable Ānanda, saying:
mn26:3.6: “Come, Ānanda, let us approach the Eastern tank to bathe our limbs.”
mn26:3.7: “Very well, reverend Sir,” venerable Ānanda replied to the Fortunate One.
mn26:3.8: Then the Fortunate One, together with venerable Ānanda, approached the Eastern tank to bathe his limbs.
mn26:3.9: After bathing and withdrawing his limbs from the Eastern tank, he stood in one robe drying his limbs.
mn26:3.10: Then venerable Ānanda said this to the Fortunate One:
mn26:3.11: “This brāhmaṇa Rammaka’s hermitage is not far, reverend Sir.
mn26:3.12: The brāhmaṇa Rammaka’s hermitage is delightful, reverend Sir,
mn26:3.13: the brāhmaṇa Rammaka’s hermitage is pleasing, reverend Sir,
mn26:3.14: it would be good, reverend Sir, if the Fortunate One would approach the brāhmaṇa Rammaka’s hermitage, taking compassion (on us).”
mn26:3.15: The Fortunate One consented by maintaining silence.
mn26:4.1: Then the Fortunate One approached the brāhmaṇa Rammaka’s hermitage.
mn26:4.2: Then at that time a great many monks were assembled in the brāhmaṇa Rammaka’s hermitage to hear talk on the Dhamma.
mn26:4.3: Then the Fortunate One stood outside the doorway waiting for the end of the conversation.
mn26:4.4: Then, understanding that the conversation had finished, after coughing, he knocked the latch.
mn26:4.5: Those monks opened the door for the Fortunate One.
mn26:4.6: Then the Fortunate One, having entered the brāhmaṇa Rammaka’s hermitage, sat down on the prepared seat.
mn26:4.7: While sitting, the Fortunate One addressed the monks,
mn26:4.8: saying: “What is the talk about, monks, amongst those who have assembled together at present? And what is the talk amongst you that was left unfinished?”
mn26:4.9: “The talk about Dhamma, reverend Sir, was in reference to the Fortunate One, and then the Fortunate One arrived.”
mn26:4.10: “It is good, monks, this is certainly suitable, monks, for you
mn26:4.11: sons of good family, who through faith have gone forth from the home to homelessness, you should assemble to talk about Dhamma.
mn26:4.12: When you have assembled together, monks, there are two things that you ought to do:
mn26:4.13: talk about the Dhamma, or maintain noble silence.
mn26:5.1: There are these two searches, monks:
mn26:5.2: a noble search, and an ignoble search.
mn26:5.3: And what, monks, is an ignoble search?
mn26:5.4: Here, monks, someone, being himself subject to birth, seeks out what is subject to birth, being himself subject to old-age, seeks out what is subject to old-age, being himself subject to sickness, seeks out what is subject to sickness, being himself subject to death, seeks out what is subject to death, being himself subject to grief, seeks out what is subject to grief, being himself subject to defilements, seeks out what is subject to defilements.
mn26:6.1: And what do you say, monks, is subject to birth?
mn26:6.2: Wife and children, monks, are subject to birth, female and male servants are subject to birth, goats and sheep are subject to birth, chickens and pigs are subject to birth, elephants, cows, horses and mares are subject to birth, gold and silver are subject to birth,
mn26:6.3: these, monks, are the bases of what is subject to birth.
mn26:6.4: Herein, tied, infatuated, and indulging in this, being himself subject to birth, he seeks out what is subject to birth,
mn26:7.1: And what do you say, monks, is subject to old-age?
mn26:7.2: Wife and children, monks, are subject to old-age, female and male servants are subject to old-age, goats and sheep are subject to old-age, chickens and pigs are subject to old-age, elephants, cows, horses and mares are subject to old-age, gold and silver are subject to old-age,
mn26:7.3: these, monks, are the bases of what is subject to old-age.
mn26:7.4: Herein, tied, infatuated, and indulging in this, being himself subject to old-age, he seeks out what is subject to old-age,
mn26:8.1: And what do you say, monks, is subject to sickness?
mn26:8.2: Wife and children, monks, are subject to sickness, female and male servants are subject to sickness, goats and sheep are subject to sickness, chickens and pigs are subject to sickness, elephants, cows, horses and mares are subject to sickness,
mn26:8.3: these, monks, are the bases of what is subject to sickness.
mn26:8.4: Herein, tied, infatuated, and indulging in this, being himself subject to sickness, he seeks out what is subject to sickness,
mn26:9.1: And what do you say, monks, is subject to death?
mn26:9.2: Wife and children, monks, are subject to death, female and male servants are subject to death, goats and sheep are subject to death, chickens and pigs are subject to death, elephants, cows, horses and mares are subject to death,
mn26:9.3: these, monks, are the bases of what is subject to death.
mn26:9.4: Herein, tied, infatuated, and indulging in this, being himself subject to death, he seeks out what is subject to death,
mn26:10.1: And what do you say, monks, is subject to grief?
mn26:10.2: Wife and children, monks, are subject to grief, female and male servants are subject to grief, goats and sheep are subject to grief, chickens and pigs are subject to grief, elephants, cows, horses and mares are subject to grief,
mn26:10.3: these, monks, are the bases of what is subject to grief.
mn26:10.4: Herein, tied, infatuated, and indulging in this, being himself subject to grief, he seeks out what is subject to grief,
mn26:11.1: And what do you say, monks, is subject to defilements?
mn26:11.2: Wife and children, monks, are subject to defilements, female and male servants are subject to defilements, goats and sheep are subject to defilements, chickens and pigs are subject to defilements, elephants, cows, horses and mares are subject to defilements, gold and silver are subject to defilements,
mn26:11.3: these, monks, are the bases of what is subject to defilements.
mn26:11.4: Herein, tied, infatuated, and indulging in this, being himself subject to defilements, he seeks out what is subject to defilements.
mn26:11.5: This, monks, is an ignoble search.
mn26:12.1: And what, monks, is a noble search?
mn26:12.2: Here, monks, someone, being himself subject to birth, after understanding the danger in being subject to birth, seeks out the birthless, supreme, secure Nibbāna, being himself subject to old-age, after understanding the danger in being subject to old-age, seeks out the ageless, supreme, secure Nibbāna, being himself subject to disease, after understanding the danger in being subject to disease, seeks out the sickless, supreme, secure Nibbāna, being himself subject to death, after understanding the danger in being subject to death, seeks out the deathless, supreme, secure Nibbāna, being himself subject to grief, after understanding the danger in being subject to grief, seeks out the griefless, supreme, secure Nibbāna, being himself subject to defilements, after understanding the danger in being subject to defilements, seeks out the undefiled, supreme, secure Nibbāna.
mn26:12.3: This, monks, is a noble search.
mn26:13.1: I also, monks, before the Awakening, while still an unawakened Bodhisatta, being myself subject to birth, sought out what was subject to birth, being myself subject to old-age, sought out what was subject to old-age, being myself subject to sickness, sought out what was subject to sickness, being myself subject to death, sought out what was subject to death, being myself subject to grief, sought out what was subject to grief, being myself subject to defilements, sought out what was subject to defilements.
mn26:13.2: Then, monks, this occurred to me:
mn26:13.3: ‘Why, being myself subject to birth, do I seek out what is subject to birth, being myself subject to old-age, do I seek out what is subject to old-age, being myself subject to disease, do I seek out what is subject to disease, being myself subject to death, do I seek out what is subject to death, being myself subject to grief, do I seek out what is subject to grief, being myself subject to defilements, do I seek out what is subject to defilements?
mn26:13.4: What if I, being myself subject to birth, after understanding the danger in being subject to birth, were to seek out the birthless, supreme, secure Nibbāna, being myself subject to old-age, after understanding the danger in being subject to old-age, were to seek out the ageless, supreme, secure Nibbāna, being myself subject to disease, after understanding the danger in being subject to disease, were to seek out the sickless, supreme, secure Nibbāna, being myself subject to death, after understanding the danger in being subject to death, were to seek out the deathless, supreme, secure Nibbāna, being myself subject to grief, after understanding the danger in being subject to grief, were to seek out the griefless, supreme, secure Nibbāna, being myself subject to defilements, after understanding the danger in being subject to defilements, were to seek out the undefiled, supreme, secure Nibbāna?’
mn26:14.1: Then at another time, monks, while still a youth, having beautiful black hair, endowed with auspicious youthfulness, in the prime of life, though my Mother and Father didn’t like it, and were crying with tearful faces, after shaving off my hair and beard, and donning brown garments, I went forth from the home to the homeless life.
mn26:15.1: When I had gone forth thus, searching for what was wholesome, the unsurpassed, noble and peaceful state, I approached Āḷāra Kālāma, and after approaching, I said this to Āḷāra Kālāma:
mn26:15.2: “I desire, friend Kālāma, to lead the spiritual life in this Dhamma and Discipline.”
mn26:15.3: When this was said, monks, Āḷāra Kālāma said this to me:
mn26:15.5: venerable, this Dhamma is such that a wise man in no long time, having deep knowledge himself of what comes from his own teacher, can live, having directly experienced and attained it.”
mn26:15.6: Then, monks, in no long time I had soon mastered that Dhamma.
mn26:15.7: Then, monks, after a little time, merely through beating my lips, merely through repeating the prattling, I spoke knowingly about that teaching and confidently about that teaching, claiming: ‘I know, I see.’ Both I and others also.
mn26:15.8: Then this occurred to me, monks:
mn26:15.9: ‘Āḷāra Kālāma did not declare: “Through mere faith in this Dhamma alone, I have deep knowledge of it myself, I live, having directly experienced and attained it,”
mn26:15.10: for sure Āḷāra Kālāma lives knowing and seeing this Dhamma.’
mn26:15.11: Then, monks, I approached Āḷāra Kālāma, and after approaching, I said this to Āḷāra Kālāma:
mn26:15.12: “In what way, friend Kālāma, do you declare: I have deep knowledge of this Dhamma myself, having directly experienced and attained it?”
mn26:15.13: When this was said, monks, Āḷāra Kālāma declared the Sphere of Nothingness.
mn26:15.14: Then, monks, this occurred to me:
mn26:15.15: ‘There is not faith for Āḷāra Kālāma (alone), for me also there is faith,
mn26:15.16: there is not energy for Āḷāra Kālāma (alone), for me also there is energy,
mn26:15.17: there is not mindfulness for Āḷāra Kālāma (alone), for me also there is mindfulness,
mn26:15.18: there is not concentration for Āḷāra Kālāma (alone), for me also there is concentration,
mn26:15.19: there is not wisdom for Āḷāra Kālāma (alone), for me also there is wisdom.
mn26:15.20: What if, in regard to the Dhamma that Āḷāra Kālāma declares: “I have deep knowledge of it myself, I live, having directly experienced and attained it,” I were to strive to realise that Dhamma?’
mn26:15.21: Then, monks, in no long time, soon having deep knowledge of that Dhamma myself, I lived, having directly experienced and attained it.
mn26:15.22: Then, monks, I approached Āḷāra Kālāma, and after approaching, I said this to Āḷāra Kālāma:
mn26:15.23: “Is it in this way, friend Kālāma, that you declare: I have deep knowledge of this Dhamma myself, having directly experienced and attained it?”
mn26:15.24: “In this way, friend, I do declare: I have deep knowledge of this Dhamma myself, having directly experienced and attained it.”
mn26:15.25: “In this way I also, friend, say: I have deep knowledge of this Dhamma myself, I live, having directly experienced and attained it.”
mn26:15.26: “It is a gain for us, friend, it is a great gain for us, friend,
mn26:15.27: that we see such a venerable with us in the spiritual life.
mn26:15.28: Thus I declare I have deep knowledge of this Dhamma myself, having directly experienced and attained it, and you have deep knowledge of this Dhamma yourself, and live, having directly experienced and attained it. You have deep knowledge of this Dhamma yourself, and live, having directly experienced and attained it,
mn26:15.29: and I declare I have deep knowledge of this Dhamma myself, having directly experienced and attained it.
mn26:15.30: Thus the Dhamma I know is the Dhamma you know, the Dhamma you know is the Dhamma I know.
mn26:15.31: Thus as I am, so are you, as you are, so am I.
mn26:15.32: Come now, friend, the two of us will look after this group.”
mn26:15.33: “Thus my teacher Āḷāra Kālāma, monks, placed me, the pupil, as equal, and in the very same position as himself, and worshipped me with the highest worship.
mn26:15.34: Then, monks, this occurred to me:
mn26:15.35: ‘This Dhamma does not lead to disenchantment, to dispassion, to cessation to peace, to deep knowledge, to Complete Awakening, to Nibbāna, but only as far as rebirth in the Sphere of Nothingness.’
mn26:15.36: Then, monks, having not found satisfaction in that Dhamma, I was therefore disgusted with that Dhamma and went away.
mn26:16.1: Then, monks, still searching for what was wholesome, the unsurpassed, noble and peaceful state, I approached Uddaka Rāmaputta, and after approaching, I said this to Uddaka Rāmaputta:
mn26:16.2: “I desire, friend, to lead the spiritual life in this Dhamma and Discipline.”
mn26:16.3: When this was said, monks, Uddaka Rāmaputta said this to me:
mn26:16.5: venerable, this Dhamma is such that a wise man in no long time, having deep knowledge himself of what comes from his own teacher, can live, having directly experienced and attained it.”
mn26:16.6: Then in no long time, monks, soon I had mastered that Dhamma.
mn26:16.7: Then, monks, after a little time I indeed, merely through beating my lips, merely through repeating the prattling, spoke knowingly about that teaching and confidently about that teaching, claiming: ‘I know, I see.’ Both I and others also.
mn26:16.8: Then, monks, this occurred to me:
mn26:16.9: ‘Rāma did not declare: “Through mere faith in this Dhamma alone, having knowledge of it myself, I live, having directly experienced and attained it,”
mn26:16.10: for sure Rāma lived knowing and seeing this Dhamma.’
mn26:16.11: Then, monks, I approached Uddaka Rāmaputta, and after approaching, I said this to Uddaka Rāmaputta:
mn26:16.12: “In what way, friend, did Rāma declare: I have deep knowledge of this Dhamma myself, having directly experienced and attained it?”
mn26:16.13: When this was said, monks, Uddaka Rāmaputta, declared the Sphere of Neither-Perception-nor-Non-Perception.
mn26:16.14: Then, monks, this occurred to me:
mn26:16.15: ‘There was not faith for Rāma (alone), for me also there is faith,
mn26:16.16: there was not energy for Rāma (alone), for me also there is energy,
mn26:16.17: there was not mindfulness for Rāma (alone), for me also there is mindfulness,
mn26:16.18: there was not concentration for Rāma (alone), for me also there is concentration,
mn26:16.19: there was not wisdom for Rāma (alone), for me also there is wisdom.
mn26:16.20: What if, in regard to the Dhamma that Rāma declared: I have deep knowledge of it myself, I live, having directly experienced and attained it, I were to strive to realise that Dhamma?’
mn26:16.21: Then, monks, in no long time, soon having deep knowledge of that Dhamma myself, I lived, having directly experienced and attained it.
mn26:16.22: Then, monks, I approached Uddaka Rāmaputta, and after approaching, I said this to Uddaka Rāmaputta:
mn26:16.23: “Is it in this way, friend, that Rāma declared: I have deep knowledge of this Dhamma myself, having directly experienced and attained it?”
mn26:16.24: “In this way, friend, Rāma did declare he had deep knowledge of this Dhamma himself, having directly experienced and attained it.”
mn26:16.25: “In this way, friend, I also say: I have deep knowledge of this Dhamma myself, I live, having directly experienced and attained it.”
mn26:16.26: “It is a gain for us, friend, it is a great gain for us, friend,
mn26:16.27: that we see such a venerable with us in the spiritual life.
mn26:16.28: Thus Rāma declared he had deep knowledge of this Dhamma himself, having directly experienced and attained it, and you have deep knowledge of this Dhamma yourself, you live, having directly experienced and attained it.
mn26:16.29: And that Dhamma you have deep knowledge of yourself, you live, having directly experienced and attained it, that Rāma declared he had deep knowledge of that Dhamma himself, having directly experienced and attained it.
mn26:16.30: Thus the Dhamma Rāma knew is the Dhamma you know, the Dhamma you know is the Dhamma Rāma knew.
mn26:16.31: Thus as Rāma was, so are you, as you are, so was Rāma.
mn26:16.32: Come now, friend, you will look after this group.”
mn26:16.33: Thus my friend in the spiritual life, Uddaka Rāmaputta, monks, placed me in the teacher’s position, and worshipped me with the highest worship.
mn26:16.34: Then, monks, this occurred to me:
mn26:16.35: ‘This Dhamma does not lead to disenchantment, or to dispassion, or to cessation, or to peace, or to deep knowledge, or to Complete Awakening, or to Nibbāna, but only as far as rebirth in the Sphere of Neither-Perception-nor-Non-Perception.’
mn26:16.36: Then, monks, having not found satisfaction in that Dhamma, I was therefore disgusted with that Dhamma and went away.
mn26:17.1: Then, monks, still searching for what was wholesome, the unsurpassed, noble and peaceful state, while walking gradually on walking tour I entered Magadha, and arrived at the Army town at Uruvelā.
mn26:17.2: There I saw a delightful piece of land, and a pleasing jungle thicket, with a clear river flowing and lovely banks, and nearby a village suitable for collecting alms.
mn26:17.3: Then, monks, this occurred to me:
mn26:17.4: ‘Delightful is this piece of land, with its pleasing jungle thicket, and a clear river flowing and lovely banks, and it is near a village suitable for collecting alms.
mn26:17.5: I thought: ‘This is surely enough for the striving of a son of a good family who is seeking to strive.’
mn26:17.6: Then, monks, I sat down right there,
mn26:18.1: Then, monks, being myself subject to birth, after understanding the danger in being subject to birth, while seeking the birthless, supreme, secure Nibbāna, I attained the birthless, supreme, secure Nibbāna, being myself subject to old-age, after understanding the danger in being subject to old-age, while seeking the ageless, supreme, secure Nibbāna, I attained the ageless, supreme, secure Nibbāna, being myself subject to sickness, after understanding the danger in being subject to sickness, while seeking the sickless, supreme, secure Nibbāna, I attained the sickless, supreme, secure Nibbāna, being myself subject to death, after understanding the danger in being subject to death, while seeking the deathless, supreme, secure Nibbāna, I attained the deathless, supreme, secure Nibbāna, being myself subject to grief, after understanding the danger in being subject to grief, while seeking the griefless, supreme, secure Nibbāna, I attained the griefless, supreme, secure Nibbāna, being myself subject to defilements, after understanding the danger in being subject to defilements, while seeking the undefiled, supreme, secure Nibbāna, I attained the undefiled, supreme, secure Nibbāna.
mn26:18.2: To me knowledge and insight arose:
mn26:18.3: Sure is my liberation of mind, this is my last birth, now there is no continuation of existence.
mn26:19.1: Then, monks, this occurred to me:
mn26:19.2: ‘This Dhamma I have attained is deep, hard to see, hard to understand, peaceful, excellent, beyond the sphere of logic, profound, understandable (only) by the wise.
mn26:19.3: But this generation delights in desire, is devoted to desire, gladdened by desire, and for this generation delighting in desire, devoted to desire, gladdened by desire,
mn26:19.4: this thing is hard to see, that is to say: conditionality and conditional origination.
mn26:19.5: This thing also is hard to see, that is to say: the tranquilising of all processes, the letting go of all bases for cleaving, the end of craving, dispassion, cessation, Nibbāna.
mn26:19.6: But if I were to teach the Dhamma and others did not understand me that would be tiring for me, that would be troublesome to me.’
mn26:19.7: Further, monks, these truly wonderful verses occurred to me, that were unheard of in the past:
mn26:19.8: ‘Now is it suitable for me to explain what was attained with difficulty?
mn26:19.10: For those overcome by passion and hatred this Dhamma is not easily understood.
mn26:19.12: Going against the stream, it is profound, deep, hard to see, subtle.
mn26:19.15: obstructed by darkness, will not see it.’
mn26:19.16: Such was my reflection, monks, and my mind inclined to inaction, not to teaching the Dhamma.
mn26:20.1: Then, monks, to Brahmā Sahampati, knowing with his mind the reflection in my mind, this (thought) occurred:
mn26:20.2: ‘The world is surely going to destruction, the world is surely going to complete destruction, wherever the Realised One, the Worthy One, the Perfect Sambuddha’s mind inclines to inaction, not to teaching the Dhamma.’
mn26:20.3: Then, monks, Brahmā Sahampati, just as a strong man might stretch out a bent arm, or bend in an outstretched arm, so did he vanish from the Brahmā world and appear in front of me.
mn26:20.4: Then, monks, Brahmā Sahampati, after arranging his upper robe on one shoulder, and raising his hands in respectful salutation, said this to me:
mn26:20.5: “Let the Fortunate One preach the Dhamma, reverend Sir, let the Happy One preach the Dhamma,
mn26:20.6: there are beings with little dust on the eyes who are perishing through not hearing the Dhamma,
mn26:20.7: there will be those who understand the Dhamma.”
mn26:20.8: Brahmā Sahampati, monks, said this and after saying this he said something more:
mn26:20.11: an impure Dhamma, invented by those still stained,
mn26:20.12: open the door to the Deathless,
mn26:20.13: let them hear the Dhamma understood by the Pure One.
mn26:20.14: As one who is standing on a rock on the top of a mountain
mn26:20.15: can see the people on all sides,
mn26:20.16: in the same way, One of Great Wisdom, having ascended
mn26:20.17: the Palace made from Dhamma, Visionary One,
mn26:20.18: look down on the people overcome by grief,
mn26:20.19: One Free of Grief, on those overcome by birth and old-age.
mn26:20.20: Rise up, O Hero, Victorious in Battle.

mn26:20.22: Let the Fortunate One teach the Dhamma,
mn26:20.23: there will be those who understand.”
mn26:21.1: Then, monks, having understood Brahmā’s request, out of kindness I looked at beings around the world with my Buddha-eye.
mn26:21.2: While looking around the world, monks, with my Buddha-eye, I saw beings having little dust on the eyes, having great dust on the eyes, having sharp faculties, having undeveloped faculties, having good conditions, having poor conditions, easy to instruct, hard to instruct, and (only) some who dwelt seeing danger in what is blameworthy and in the next world.
mn26:21.3: Just as with water-lilies or lotuses or white lotuses some of those water-lilies or lotuses or white lotuses, born in the water, flourishing in the water, not rising above water, are nourished from inside the depths, some of those water-lilies or lotuses or white lotuses, born in the water, flourishing in the water, surrounded by water, stand level with the water, some of those water-lilies or lotuses or white lotuses, born in the water, flourishing in the water, stand above the water, and are untouched by the water.
mn26:21.4: Even so while looking around the world, monks, with my Buddha-eye, I saw beings having little dust on the eyes, having great dust on the eyes, having sharp faculties, having undeveloped faculties, having good conditions, having poor conditions, easy to instruct, hard to instruct, and (only) some who dwelt seeing danger in what is blameworthy and in the next world.
mn26:21.5: Then, monks, I recited this verse to Brahmā Sahampati:
mn26:21.6: “Open for you are the doors to the Deathless,
mn26:21.7: whoever has ears let them release their faith.
mn26:21.8: Perceiving trouble, Brahmā, I did not speak amongst humans,
mn26:21.9: about what was hard-learned, the excellent Dhamma!”
mn26:21.10: Then, monks, Brahmā Sahampati, thinking: ‘I have obtained consent for the Fortunate One to teach the Dhamma,’ after worshipping and circumambulating me, vanished right there.
mn26:22.1: Then, monks, this occurred to me:
mn26:22.2: ‘To whom should I first teach the Dhamma?
mn26:22.3: Who will be able to understand the Dhamma quickly?’
mn26:22.4: Then, monks, this occurred to me:
mn26:22.5: ‘This Āḷāra Kālāma is wise, learned, intelligent, for a long time he has been one with little dust on his eyes.
mn26:22.6: Now what if I first teach the Dhamma to Āḷāra Kālāma?
mn26:22.7: He will be able to understand the Dhamma quickly.’
mn26:22.8: Then a god, monks, having approached, said this to me:
mn26:22.9: “Āḷāra Kālāma died seven days ago, reverend Sir,”
mn26:22.10: and to me knowledge and insight arose:
mn26:22.12: Then, monks, this occurred to me:
mn26:22.14: if he had heard this Dhamma he would have understood it quickly.’
mn26:23.1: Then, monks, this occurred to me:
mn26:23.2: ‘To whom should I first teach the Dhamma?
mn26:23.3: Who will be able to understand the Dhamma quickly?’
mn26:23.4: Then, monks, this occurred to me:
mn26:23.5: ‘This Uddaka Rāmaputta is wise, learned, intelligent, for a long time he has been one with little dust on his eyes.
mn26:23.6: Now, what if I first teach the Dhamma to Uddaka Rāmaputta?
mn26:23.7: He will be able to understand the Dhamma quickly.’
mn26:23.8: Then, monks, a god having approached, said this to me:
mn26:23.9: “Uddaka Rāmaputta died yesterday evening, reverend Sir,”
mn26:23.10: and to me knowledge and insight arose:
mn26:23.12: Then, monks, this occurred to me:
mn26:23.14: if he had heard this Dhamma he would have understood it quickly.’
mn26:24.1: Then, monks, this occurred to me:
mn26:24.2: ‘To whom should I first teach the Dhamma?
mn26:24.3: Who will be able to understand the Dhamma quickly?’
mn26:24.4: Then, monks, this occurred to me:
mn26:24.5: ‘The group-of-five monks were very helpful to me, they attended on me when I was striving resolutely.
mn26:24.6: Now, what if I first teach the Dhamma to the group-of-five monks?’
mn26:24.7: Then, monks, this occurred to me:
mn26:24.8: ‘Where are the group-of-five monks dwelling right now?’
mn26:24.9: I saw with the divine eye, monks, which is purified and surpasses that of (normal) men, that the group-of-five monks were dwelling near Bārāṇasī, in the Deer Park at Isipatana.
mn26:24.10: Then, monks, having dwelt for as long as I liked I left on walking tour for Bārāṇasī.
mn26:25.1: The Abstainer Upaka saw me, monks, going along the highway between the Bodhi (tree) and Gayā,
mn26:25.2: and after seeing (me), he said this to me:
mn26:25.3: “Your faculties, friend, are very clear, purified is your skin and bright,
mn26:25.4: on account of whom, friend, did you go forth, or who is your teacher, or what Dhamma do you prefer?”
mn26:25.5: When this was said, monks, I addressed the Abstainer Upaka with verses:
mn26:25.7: undefiled in regard to all things,
mn26:25.8: having given up everything, liberated through the destruction of craving,
mn26:25.9: having deep knowledge myself, who should I point to (as Teacher)?
mn26:25.10: There is no Teacher for me,
mn26:25.11: no one like me is found,
mn26:25.12: there is no person equal to me in the world with its gods.
mn26:25.14: I am a Worthy One in the world, I am the Unsurpassed Teacher,
mn26:25.16: I am the One Perfect Sambuddha,
mn26:25.18: I go to Kāsī’s city to set the Dhamma-Wheel rolling,
mn26:25.20: I will beat the drum of the Deathless in a world that is blind.”
mn26:25.22: “It is as if you declare, friend, you are a Worthy One, an Infinite Victor!”
mn26:25.24: who have attained the destruction of the pollutants.
mn26:25.25: I have been victorious over all wicked things,
mn26:25.26: therefore, Upaka, I am a Victor.”
mn26:25.27: When this was said, monks, the Abstainer Upaka, after saying: “It may be so, friend,” shaking his head, and taking the wrong path, went away.
mn26:26.1: Then, monks, while I was walking gradually on walking tour, I approached Bārāṇasī, Isipatana, the Deer Park, and the group-of-five monks.
mn26:26.2: The group-of-five monks, monks, saw me coming from afar,
mn26:26.3: and after seeing (me), they resolved among themselves:
mn26:26.4: “This Ascetic Gotama who is coming, friends, is given to luxury, forsaking the striving he has gone back to luxury.
mn26:26.5: He should certainly not be worshipped or stood up for, nor should his bowl and robe be taken,
mn26:26.6: however, we can prepare a seat, if he wishes he will sit down.”
mn26:26.7: As I approached, monks, the group-of-five monks were unable to continue with their own agreement,
mn26:26.8: and after coming out to meet me, some took my bowl and robe, some prepared the seat, some placed the water (for washing) the feet.
mn26:26.9: Then they addressed me by name and with the word ‘friend’.
mn26:27.1: When this was said, monks, I said this to the group-of-five monks:
mn26:27.2: “Do not address the Fortunate One, monks, by name and by the word ‘friend’,
mn26:27.3: the Realised One is a Worthy One, monks, a Perfect Sambuddha.
mn26:27.4: Lend an ear, monks, I will instruct you about the attainment of the Deathless, I will teach the Dhamma,
mn26:27.5: (and) following the path as it has been preached, after no long time you will (attain) that good for which young men of good family rightly go forth from the home to the homeless life, that unsurpassed conclusion to the spiritual life, you will dwell having known, experienced, and attained it yourselves in this very life.”
mn26:27.6: When this was said, the group-of-five monks said this to me:
mn26:27.7: “But you, friend Gotama, by that (ascetic) lifestyle, that practice, that difficult way of living, did not attain states beyond (ordinary) human beings, a distinction of what is truly noble knowledge and insight. So how can you now, given to luxury, forsaking the striving, gone back to luxury, attain states beyond (ordinary) human beings, a distinction of what is truly noble knowledge and insight?”
mn26:27.8: When this was said, monks, I said this to the group-of-five monks:
mn26:27.9: “The Realised One, monks, is not given to luxury, is not forsaking the striving, and has not gone back to luxury,
mn26:27.10: the Realised One, monks, is a Worthy One, a Perfect Sambuddha.
mn26:27.11: Lend an ear, monks, I will instruct you about the attainment of the Deathless, I will teach the Dhamma, (and) following the path as it has been preached,
mn26:27.12: after no long time (you will attain) that good for which young men of good family rightly go forth from the home to the homeless life, that unsurpassed conclusion to the spiritual life, you will dwell having known, experienced, and attained it yourselves in this very life.”
mn26:27.13: For a second time the group-of-five monks said this to me:
mn26:27.14: “But you, friend Gotama, by that (ascetic) lifestyle, that practice, that difficult way of living, did not attain states beyond (ordinary) human beings, a distinction of what is truly noble knowledge and insight. So how can you now, given to luxury, forsaking the striving, gone back to luxury, attain a state beyond (ordinary) human beings, a distinction of what is truly noble knowledge and insight?”
mn26:27.15: For a second time, monks, I said this to the group-of-five monks:
mn26:27.16: “The Realised One, monks, is not given to luxury, is not forsaking the striving, and has not gone back to luxury, the Realised One, monks, is a Worthy One, a Perfect Sambuddha. Lend an ear, monks, I will instruct you about the attainment of the Deathless, I will teach the Dhamma, (and) following the path as it has been preached, after no long time in regard to that good for which young men of good family rightly go forth from the home to the homeless life, that unsurpassed conclusion to the spiritual life,
mn26:27.17: you will dwell having known, experienced, and attained it yourselves in this very life.”
mn26:27.18: For a third time the group-of-five monks said this to me:
mn26:27.19: “But you, friend Gotama, by that (ascetic) lifestyle, that practice, that difficult way of living, did not attain states beyond (ordinary) human beings, a distinction of what is truly noble knowledge and insight. So how can you now, given to luxury, forsaking the striving, gone back to luxury, attain states beyond (ordinary) human beings, a distinction of what is truly noble knowledge and insight?”
mn26:28.1: When this was said, monks, I said this to the group-of-five monks:
mn26:28.2: “Are you aware, monks, of my having spoken to you like this before?”
mn26:28.4: “The Realised One, monks, is a Worthy One, a Perfect Sambuddha.
mn26:28.5: Lend an ear, monks, I will instruct you about the attainment of the Deathless, I will teach the Dhamma, (and) following the path as it has been preached,
mn26:28.6: after no long time in regard to that good for which young men of good family rightly go forth from the home to the homeless life, that unsurpassed conclusion to the spiritual life, you will dwell having known, experienced, and attained it yourselves in this very life,”
mn26:29.1: and I was able, monks, to persuade the group-of-five monks.
mn26:29.2: Then, monks, I advised two monks and three monks wandered for alms,
mn26:29.3: and the group of six monks subsisted on whatever, after walking for alms-food, the three monks brought them.
mn26:29.4: Then, monks, I advised three monks and two monks wandered for alms,
mn26:29.5: and the group of six monks subsisted on whatever, after walking for alms-food, the two monks brought them.
mn26:30.1: Then, monks, the group-of-five monks, while being advised by me, while being instructed, being themselves subject to birth, after understanding the danger in being subject to birth, while seeking the birthless, supreme, secure Nibbāna, attained the birthless, supreme, secure Nibbāna, being themselves subject to old-age, after understanding the danger in being subject to old-age, while seeking the ageless, supreme, secure Nibbāna, attained the ageless, supreme, secure Nibbāna, being themselves subject to sickness, after understanding the danger in being subject to sickness, while seeking the sickless, supreme, secure Nibbāna, attained the sickless, supreme, secure Nibbāna, being themselves subject to death, after understanding the danger in being subject to death, while seeking the deathless, supreme, secure Nibbāna, attained the deathless, supreme, secure Nibbāna, being themselves subject to grief, after understanding the danger in being subject to grief, while seeking the griefless, supreme, secure Nibbāna, attained the griefless, supreme, secure Nibbāna, being themselves subject to defilements, after understanding the danger in being subject to defilements, while seeking the undefiled, supreme, secure Nibbāna, attained the undefiled, supreme, secure Nibbāna.
mn26:30.2: To them knowledge and insight arose: Sure is my liberation of mind,
mn26:30.3: this is my last birth, now there is no continuation of existence.
mn26:31.1: There are these five strands, monks, of sense pleasure.
mn26:31.3: Forms cognizable by the eye, which are wanted, lovely, pleasant, likeable, sensual, enticing,
mn26:31.4: sounds cognizable by the ear, which are wanted, lovely, pleasant, likeable, sensual, enticing,
mn26:31.5: smells cognizable by the nose, which are wanted, lovely, pleasant, likeable, sensual, enticing,
mn26:31.7: which are wanted, lovely, pleasant, likeable, sensual, enticing, tangibles cognizable by the body, which are wanted, lovely, pleasant, likeable, sensual, enticing,
mn26:31.8: these, monks, are the five strands of sense pleasure.
mn26:32.1: Whichever ascetics or brāhmaṇas, monks, are tied, infatuated, and indulging in these five strands of sense pleasure, who use them not seeing the danger in them, not knowing the escape from them, of them this should be known:
mn26:32.2: ‘They have fallen upon misfortune, they have fallen upon destruction, the Wicked One can do whatever he likes (with them).’
mn26:32.3: Just as, monks, if there were a wild deer lying bound in a snare,
mn26:32.5: ‘He has fallen upon misfortune, he has fallen upon destruction, the hunter can do whatever he likes (with him),
mn26:32.6: and when the hunter comes he cannot depart as he desires.’
mn26:32.7: Just so, monks, whichever ascetics or brāhmaṇas are tied, infatuated, and indulging in these five strands of sense pleasure, who use them not seeing the danger in them, not knowing the escape from them, of them this should be known:
mn26:32.8: ‘They have fallen upon misfortune, they have fallen upon destruction, the Wicked One can do whatever he likes (with them).’
mn26:33.1: And, monks, whichever ascetics or brāhmaṇas are not tied, not infatuated, and do not indulge in these five strands of sense pleasure, who use them seeing the danger in them, knowing the escape from them, of them this should be known:
mn26:33.2: ‘They have not fallen upon misfortune, they have not fallen upon destruction, the Wicked One cannot do whatever he likes (with them).’
mn26:33.3: Just as, monks, if there were a wild deer not lying bound in a snare,
mn26:33.5: ‘He has not fallen upon misfortune, he has not fallen upon destruction, the hunter cannot do whatever he likes (with him),
mn26:33.6: and when the hunter comes he can depart as he desires.’
mn26:33.7: Just so, monks, whichever ascetics or brāhmaṇas are not tied, not infatuated, and do not indulge in these five strands of sense pleasure, who use them seeing the danger in them, knowing the escape from them, of them this should be known:
mn26:33.8: ‘They have not fallen upon misfortune, they have not fallen upon destruction, the Wicked One cannot do whatever he likes (with them).’
mn26:34.1: Just as, monks, if there were a wild deer wandering in a forest wilderness, he goes confidently, he stands confidently, he sits confidently, he lies down confidently.
mn26:34.2: What is the reason for that?
mn26:34.3: He is not, monks, within the range of a hunter.
mn26:34.4: Just so, monks, a monk quite secluded from sense desires, secluded from unwholesome things, having thinking, reflection, and the happiness and rapture born of seclusion, dwells having attained the first absorption.
mn26:34.5: It is said of this monk, monks, he has made Māra blind and footless, he has destroyed Māra’s eye, the Wicked One wanders without seeing (him).
mn26:35.1: Furthermore, monks, a monk, with the ending of thinking and reflection, with internal clarity, and one-pointedness of mind, being without thinking, without reflection, having the happiness and rapture born of concentration, dwells having attained the second absorption.
mn26:35.2: It is said of this monk, monks, he has made Māra blind and footless, he has destroyed Māra’s eye, the Wicked One wanders without seeing (him).
mn26:36.1: Furthermore, monks, a monk, with the fading away of rapture dwells equanimous, mindful, clearly knowing, experiencing happiness through the body, about which the Noble Ones declare: “He lives pleasantly, mindful, and equanimous,” (thus) he dwells having attained the third absorption.
mn26:36.2: It is said of this monk, monks, he has made Māra blind and footless, he has destroyed Māra’s eye, the Wicked One wanders without seeing (him).
mn26:37.1: Furthermore, monks, a monk, having given up pleasure, given up pain, and with the previous disappearence of mental well-being and sorrow, without pain, without pleasure, and with complete purity of mindfulness owing to equanimity, dwells having attained the fourth absorption.
mn26:37.2: It is said of this monk, monks, he has made Māra blind and footless, he has destroyed Māra’s eye, the Wicked One wanders without seeing (him).
mn26:38.1: Furthermore, monks, a monk, having completely transcended perceptions of form, with the disappearance of perceptions of (sensory) impact, not attending to perceptions of variety, (understanding): ‘This is endless space’, abides in the sphere of endless space.
mn26:38.2: It is said of this monk, monks, he has made Māra blind and footless, he has destroyed Māra’s eye, the Wicked One wanders without seeing (him).
mn26:39.1: Furthermore, monks, a monk, having completely transcended the sphere of endless space, (understanding): ‘This is endless consciousness,’ abides in the sphere of endless consciousness.
mn26:39.2: It is said of this monk, monks, he has made Māra blind and footless, he has destroyed Māra’s eye, the Wicked One wanders without seeing (him).
mn26:40.1: Furthermore, monks, a monk, having completely transcended the sphere of endless consciousness, (understanding): ‘This is nothing,’ abides in the sphere of nothingness.
mn26:40.2: It is said of this monk, monks, he has made Māra blind and footless, he has destroyed Māra’s eye, the Wicked One wanders without seeing (him).
mn26:41.1: Furthermore, monks, a monk, having completely transcended the sphere of nothingness, abides in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
mn26:41.2: It is said of this monk, monks, he has made Māra blind and footless, he has destroyed Māra’s eye, the Wicked One wanders without seeing (him).
mn26:42.1: Furthermore, monks, a monk, having completely transcended the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, abides in the cessation of perception and feeling, and having seen with wisdom, his pollutants are totally destroyed.
mn26:42.2: It is said of this monk, monks, he has made Māra blind and footless, he has destroyed Māra’s eye, the Wicked One wanders without seeing (him).
mn26:42.3: He has crossed over the world, he goes confidently, he stands confidently, he sits confidently, he lies down confidently.
mn26:42.4: What is the reason for that?
mn26:42.5: He is not within the range, monks, of the Wicked One.
mn26:42.7: and those monks were uplifted and greatly rejoiced in what was said by the Fortunate One.
